title: Lichtenhainer Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: Lichtenhainer is a smoky, sour, low alcohol German beer. Learn its history, how it tastes and how brewers recreate it today.
teaser: Smoke and sourness in one light glass. Lichtenhainer is the strangest German beer most people have never tried.
standfirst: Lichtenhainer is a historical German beer that is both smoked and sour, at well under 5% ABV. It nearly vanished in the twentieth century and survives today mainly through curious brewers. Here is what it was, what it tastes like and why it is worth seeking out.
sections:
Lichtenhainer is named after Lichtenhain, a village near the university town of Jena in Thuringia, central Germany. It was a local everyday beer, drunk widely by students and townspeople in the nineteenth century. Like many regional German styles, it faded as pale lager spread and largely disappeared in the twentieth century.

Brewers revived it in recent decades, guided by historical descriptions. The BJCP now lists Lichtenhainer among its historical styles, alongside other rescued beers such as gose and Kentucky common.

What makes Lichtenhainer unusual is the combination. It was brewed with smoked malt, a common feature of old German brewing when malt was dried over wood fires. It was also sour, thanks to lactic acid bacteria working alongside the yeast. Most beers carry one of those features. Lichtenhainer carries both.

The modern guideline describes a beer of roughly 3.5 to 4.7% ABV, with low bitterness, moderate smoke and clean lactic sourness. It is pale gold to light amber and often a little hazy. Some versions use wheat malt for part of the grist, which gives a soft, bready body.
How smoke and acid change each other

You might expect smoke and sourness to clash. In practice they balance. The acidity keeps the smoke from turning heavy or ashy. The smoke gives the sourness a savoury depth that plain sour wheat beers lack. A good Lichtenhainer tastes a little like a tart, smoky lemonade with bread underneath.

The smoke should stay moderate. Brewers usually use beechwood-smoked malt in a smaller share than in a Bamberg rauchbier. Too much and the beer tastes like a campfire with vinegar poured over it.

A modern Lichtenhainer grist often combines pilsner malt, wheat malt and a portion of smoked malt. Souring is usually done in the kettle with Lactobacillus, held at around 35 to 45 °C until the wort reaches a pH near 3.4 to 3.6. The wort is then boiled and fermented with a clean ale yeast.

Some brewers prefer co-pitching yeast and bacteria for a slower, softer sourness, closer to how the beer was probably made historically. Either way, hops play almost no part. Bitterness above about 10 IBU would get in the way of the acid and smoke.

Lichtenhainer has a natural home next to Indian food. Tandoori dishes already carry char and smoke. Chaat and pickles already carry sourness. A light, tart, smoky beer picks up both without overwhelming them. Try it with tandoori chicken, smoked baingan bharta or a plate of seekh kebabs.

It is also low enough in alcohol to suit a long lunch in hot weather. The one problem is availability. Few breweries in India make it, so you may need to taste it at a festival or brew a small batch yourself.
Why smoked malt was once ordinary

Before indirect kilns became common, maltsters often dried green malt over open fires. Smoke from the fuel passed straight through the grain, so many old beers carried some smoke whether brewers wanted it or not. Lichtenhainer is one of the styles that kept that character after most beers lost it.

Bamberg in Franconia is the best known place where smoky beer survived, with its beechwood-smoked rauchbier. Poland has grodziskie, a light oak-smoked wheat beer of roughly 2.5 to 3.3% ABV that is smoky but not sour. Lichtenhainer is the odd one out among these smoked survivors because it is also tart.

Comparing them is revealing. Grodziskie shows smoke on a dry, bitter wheat base. Rauchbier shows smoke on a rich lager. Lichtenhainer shows smoke on a sour wheat base. Same idea, three very different beers, each shaped by local grain, local wood and local taste.
Learning to taste two flavours at once

Lichtenhainer is a good test of a taster. You need to judge the smoke and the acidity separately, then decide whether they work together. Is the smoke clean, like ham or beechwood, or harsh, like ashtray? Is the acidity clean lactic, or does it carry vinegar? Separating layered flavours like this is exactly what structured sensory training builds.

A simple first step: taste a smoked beer and a sour wheat beer side by side, then blend a small amount of each in a third glass. You will have made a rough Lichtenhainer at the table and learned how the two flavours interact.
faqs: It is light, tart and moderately smoky, with a bready wheat body and very low bitterness.
